title: Ἀμφ’ Ἀλκαθόῳ
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Deiphobus, unsure whether to face the Achaeans alone or fetch help, goes to Aeneas, who stands at the back of the Trojan throng because Priam has never honoured him, and calls on him to defend his brother-in-law Alcathous, whom Idomeneus has just killed. Aeneas comes, and Idomeneus calls five companions to him and stands like a boar at bay; the two sides close over the body of Alcathous. Aeneas casts at Idomeneus and misses; Idomeneus kills Oenomaus, and Deiphobus, missing Idomeneus, kills Ascalaphus, a son of Ares, who sits on Olympus not yet knowing it. Meriones wounds Deiphobus and his brother Polites takes him off to the city, while Aeneas and Antilochus each kill a man, and Antilochus is kept unharmed by Poseidon.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Δηΐφοβος δὲ διάνδιχα μερμήριξεν
ἤ τινά που Τρώων ἑταρίσσαιτο μεγαθύμων
ἂψ ἀναχωρήσας, ἦ πειρήσαιτο καὶ οἶος.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Dēïphobos de diandicha mermērixen
ē tina pou Trōōn hetarissaito megathymōn
aps anachōrēsas, ē peirēsaito kai oios.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Deiphobus in two ways was in doubt,
whether some one, perhaps, of the great-hearted Trojans he should make his comrade,
stepping back, or should make trial even alone.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Deiphobus was in doubt between two courses: whether to step back and make one of the great-hearted Trojans his companion, or to make the attempt even alone.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes Idomeneus’ speech in the previous part, and Deiphobus, whom he addressed, now has to choose. διάνδιχα μερμήριξεν ‘was in doubt between two courses’ is the same phrase as at 1.189 and is translated the same; the two courses follow, as ἤ … ἦ ‘whether … or’ (ἦ is printed with a circumflex here, but it is the same ‘or’). ἑταρίσσαιτο is the aorist optative middle of ἑταρίζω ‘make a companion’, in an indirect question; τινά που ‘some one, perhaps’; ἀναχωρήσας ‘stepping back’, i.e. going back from the front to fetch him. πειρήσαιτο ‘make a trial’ has no object in the Greek. οἶος is the epic form of μόνος ‘alone’.

sentences.t:
ὧδε δέ οἱ φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι
βῆναι ἐπ’ Αἰνείαν·
sentences.tr:
hōde de hoi phroneonti doassato kerdion einai
bēnai ep’ Aineian·
sentences.l:
And thus to him considering it seemed better to be
to go to Aeneas;
sentences.i: And this, as he thought it over, seemed to him the better course: to go to Aeneas;
sentences.n: Deiphobus decides on the first of his two courses: to fetch a companion, and the one he picks is Aeneas. δοάσσατο ‘it seemed’ is an epic aorist found only in this kind of phrase; κέρδιον is a comparative, ‘better, more profitable’; φρονέοντι is the uncontracted participle (= φρονοῦντι) in the dative with οἱ ‘to him’. The line is word for word the Odyssey’s, and is translated the same. βῆναι is the aorist infinitive of βαίνω ‘go’, and ἐπ’ Αἰνείαν ‘to Aeneas’ gives the goal. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὕστατον εὗρεν ὁμίλου
ἑσταότ’·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ hystaton heuren homilou
hestaot’·
sentences.l:
and him last of the throng he found
standing;
sentences.i: and he found him standing at the very rear of the throng;
sentences.n: τόν ‘him’ is Aeneas, the pronoun picking up the last word of the line before. ὕστατον ὁμίλου ‘last of the throng’: ὕστατος ‘last’ with the genitive ὁμίλου ‘of the throng’ (ὅμιλος), i.e. at the back of the crowd, far from the front. εὗρεν is the aorist of εὑρίσκω; ἑσταότ’ is the elided accusative of the perfect participle ἑσταώς ‘standing’. The unit begins in mid-line and ends at the ano teleia after the first word of 460.

sentences.t:
αἰεὶ γὰρ Πριάμῳ ἐπεμήνιε δίῳ
οὕνεκ’ ἄρ’ ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα μετ’ ἀνδράσιν οὔ τι τίεσκεν.
sentences.tr:
aiei gar Priamōi epemēnie diōi
hounek’ ar’ esthlon eonta met’ andrasin ou ti tiesken.
sentences.l:
for always against Priam he was wrathful, heavenly Priam,
because, being good among men, he did not at all honour him.
sentences.i: for he was always wrathful against heavenly Priam, because Priam did not honour him at all, good man though he was among men.
sentences.n: This is why Aeneas stands at the back. ἐπεμήνιε is the imperfect of ἐπιμηνίω ‘bear wrath against’, the verb of μῆνις ‘wrath’, the poem’s first word, with the dative Πριάμῳ. δίῳ ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet, translated though the king is the object of Aeneas’ grudge. ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα ‘being good’ is accusative: it can only be Aeneas, the object of τίεσκεν, though the clause names no one. τίεσκεν is an iterative imperfect in -σκ- of τίω ‘honour’ (‘never honoured’), and οὔ τι means ‘not at all’. οὕνεκ’ is ὅτι ‘because’.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and, standing close beside him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: Deiphobus is about to speak. ἀγχοῦ ‘near’ and ἱστάμενος ‘standing’ (present participle middle of ἵστημι) put him at Aeneas’ side. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the stock phrase for words that fly from speaker to hearer; ἔπεα is the epic plural of ἔπος, and προσηύδα ‘he addressed’ is the imperfect of προσαυδάω. The line is the stock line of speech introduction, translated as before; its second half, ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα, also ends the line at 480 below.

sentences.t:
Αἰνεία Τρώων βουληφόρε νῦν σε μάλα χρὴ
γαμβρῷ ἀμυνέμεναι, εἴ πέρ τί σε κῆδος ἱκάνει.
sentences.tr:
Aineia Trōōn boulēphore nyn se mala chrē
gambrōi amynemenai, ei per ti se kēdos hikanei.
sentences.l:
“Aeneas, counsel-bearer of the Trojans, now you very much must
your brother-in-law defend, if only some concern reaches you.
sentences.i: “Aeneas, counsellor of the Trojans, now you most certainly must defend your brother-in-law, if any concern touches you at all.
sentences.n: Deiphobus’ appeal is to kinship. Αἰνεία is the vocative of Αἰνείας; βουληφόρε ‘counsel-bearer’ (‘counsellor’), a title of respect. νῦν σε μάλα χρή: χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the accusative σε and the infinitive ἀμυνέμεναι (epic -έμεναι = -εῖν), with the dative γαμβρῷ ‘for/to your brother-in-law’: ἀμύνω with a person in the dative and no thing warded off is ‘defend’. γαμβρός is any man related by marriage; this one is Alcathous, who married Hippodameia, the eldest daughter of Anchises (13.427–429), and Aeneas is Anchises’ son (2.819–820), so he is Aeneas’ sister’s husband. κῆδος is ‘concern, care’ and also the tie made by marriage, so the word points back to γαμβρός. ἱκάνει ‘comes to, reaches’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἕπευ Ἀλκαθόῳ ἐπαμύνομεν, ὅς σε πάρος γε
γαμβρὸς ἐὼν ἔθρεψε δόμοις ἔνι τυτθὸν ἐόντα·
sentences.tr:
all’ hepeu Alkathoōi epamynomen, hos se paros ge
gambros eōn ethrepse domois eni tytthon eonta·
sentences.l:
But follow, let us come to the defence of Alcathous, who you before
being a brother-in-law reared in his house when you were small;
sentences.i: But follow me, and let us come to the defence of Alcathous, who, as your brother-in-law, reared you in his house when you were small;
sentences.n: The reason for the appeal: Alcathous reared Aeneas. ἕπευ is the present imperative middle of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ (= ἕπου). ἐπαμύνομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘let us defend’ (‘come to the defence of’), with the dative Ἀλκαθόῳ. ὅς σε πάρος γε ‘who, in the past, you’: the relative’s object σε waits for its verb ἔθρεψε, aorist of τρέφω ‘rear’. γαμβρὸς ἐὼν ‘being a brother-in-law’ (see 464); δόμοις ἔνι ‘in the house’ (the poetic plural); τυτθὸν ἐόντα ‘being small’ agrees with σε.

sentences.t: τὸν δέ τοι Ἰδομενεὺς δουρικλυτὸς ἐξενάριξεν.
sentences.tr: ton de toi Idomeneus douriklytos exenarixen.
sentences.l: and him, you see, Idomeneus, famed-for-the-spear, despoiled.”
sentences.i: Idomeneus, famed for his spear, has killed him and stripped him of his armour.”
sentences.n: The speech ends with the news that has made the matter urgent. τόν ‘him’ is Alcathous, killed at 13.434–441; τοι is a particle, ‘you see’. δουρικλυτός ‘famed for his spear’ is the stock epithet of Idomeneus, translated every time. ἐξενάριξεν is from ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip of armour’ (ἐνάρα ‘spoils’), the verb kept the same in English each time; the stripping of Alcathous is not narrated in the previous part, and the Greek verb only says that Idomeneus is the victor over the body.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὄρινε,
βῆ δὲ μετ’ Ἰδομενῆα μέγα πτολέμοιο μεμηλώς.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, tōi d’ ara thymon eni stēthessin orine,
bē de met’ Idomenēa mega ptolemoio memēlōs.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and in him the heart in his breast he stirred,
and he went after Idomeneus, greatly concerned with war.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he stirred the heart in Aeneas’ breast, and Aeneas went after Idomeneus, greatly concerned with war.
sentences.n: The appeal works. τῷ ‘in him’ is Aeneas, the man addressed, not the speaker; the first line is a stock closing line for a speech that moves its hearer, and is translated the same with the hearer’s name. ὄρινε is the aorist of ὀρίνω ‘stir’. βῆ is the epic form of ἔβη ‘went’, and μετ’ Ἰδομενῆα ‘after Idomeneus’ is the goal he is seeking. μέγα πτολέμοιο μεμηλώς ‘greatly concerned with war’ is the perfect participle of μέλω with the genitive; πτολέμοιο is the epic form of πολέμου. The second line is word for word the one said of Meriones at 13.297 and is translated the same.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ Ἰδομενῆα φόβος λάβε τηλύγετον ὥς,
ἀλλ’ ἔμεν’ ὡς ὅτε τις σῦς οὔρεσιν ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς,
ὅς τε μένει κολοσυρτὸν ἐπερχόμενον πολὺν ἀνδρῶν
χώρῳ ἐν οἰοπόλῳ, φρίσσει δέ τε νῶτον ὕπερθεν·
sentences.tr:
all’ ouk Idomenēa phobos labe tēlygeton hōs,
all’ emen’ hōs hote tis sys ouresin alki pepoithōs,
hos te menei kolosyrton eperchomenon polyn andrōn
chōrōi en oiopolōi, phrissei de te nōton hyperthen·
sentences.l:
But not Idomeneus did fear seize, like a late-born child,
but he stood firm, as when some boar in the mountains, trusting in its might,
which awaits an uproar coming on, a great one, of men,
in a place that is lonely, and bristles, as to the back, above;
sentences.i: But fear did not seize Idomeneus as it seizes a late-born child; he stood his ground, like a boar in the mountains, trusting in its might, that waits for the great uproar of men coming on, in a lonely place, and bristles along its back;
sentences.n: Idomeneus is not frightened. ἀλλ’ οὐκ … φόβος λάβε ‘but fear did not seize’; τηλύγετον ὥς ‘like a late-born child’: the origin of τηλύγετος is not known and ‘late-born’ is the traditional gloss; the sense here is of a child who would be seized by fear. ἔμεν’ is ἔμενε, ‘stood firm’, the imperfect of μένω, which in the simile becomes the present μένει ‘awaits’. οὔρεσιν is the epic dative plural of ὄρος ‘mountain’; ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς ‘trusting in its might’ (epic dative ἀλκί). κολοσυρτὸν … πολὺν ἀνδρῶν ‘a great uproar of men’, the noise of a crowd closing in. οἰοπόλῳ ‘lonely’ is the traditional gloss; the exact sense is not certain. φρίσσει νῶτον ὕπερθεν: the accusative says where it bristles, ‘as to the back’. ὅς τε is the relative with epic τε, marking a general truth.

sentences.t: ὀφθαλμὼ δ’ ἄρα οἱ πυρὶ λάμπετον·
sentences.tr: ophthalmō d’ ara hoi pyri lampeton·
sentences.l: and the two eyes to it with fire shine;
sentences.i: and its two eyes shine with fire;
sentences.n: ὀφθαλμώ ‘the two eyes’ and λάμπετον ‘the two shine’ are duals, the Greek number for a natural pair. οἱ ‘to it’ is the dative of possession (the boar’s eyes); πυρί ‘with fire’ is a dative of means, so the eyes are lit by fire rather than merely ‘like’ it. The unit ends at the ano teleia after λάμπετον and the sentence goes on.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὀδόντας
θήγει, ἀλέξασθαι μεμαὼς κύνας ἠδὲ καὶ ἄνδρας·
sentences.tr:
autar odontas
thēgei, alexasthai memaōs kynas ēde kai andras·
sentences.l:
but its teeth
it whets, eager to defend itself against dogs and also men;
sentences.i: but it whets its teeth, eager to defend itself against both dogs and men;
sentences.n: ὀδόντας ‘teeth’ are the boar’s tusks, though the Greek says only ‘teeth’. θήγει ‘whets, sharpens’; ἀλέξασθαι is the aorist infinitive middle of ἀλέξω ‘ward off’, and in the middle with an accusative it is ‘defend oneself against’; μεμαώς, perfect participle of μάω ‘be eager’. κύνας ἠδὲ καὶ ἄνδρας ‘dogs and also men’. The unit begins in mid-line, at αὐτάρ.

sentences.t:
ὣς μένεν Ἰδομενεὺς δουρικλυτός, οὐδ’ ὑπεχώρει,
Αἰνείαν ἐπιόντα βοηθόον·
sentences.tr:
hōs menen Idomeneus douriklytos, oud’ hypechōrei,
Aineian epionta boēthoon·
sentences.l:
So stood firm Idomeneus, famed-for-the-spear, and did not give way,
before Aeneas coming on, the helper;
sentences.i: So Idomeneus, famed for his spear, stood his ground and did not give way before Aeneas, who came on to help;
sentences.n: The simile is closed: ὣς ‘so’ answers ὡς ὅτε ‘as when’ at 471, and μένεν = ἔμενε is the same verb that was ‘stood firm’ in the boar’s picture. δουρικλυτός ‘famed for his spear’. ὑπεχώρει is the imperfect of ὑποχωρέω ‘give ground’, here with the accusative Αἰνείαν ‘before Aeneas’. ἐπιόντα ‘coming on’; βοηθόον ‘helper’, from βοή ‘cry’ and θέω ‘run’, one who runs to the shout, so Aeneas comes as Deiphobus asked. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὖε δ’ ἑταίρους
Ἀσκάλαφόν τ’ ἐσορῶν Ἀφαρῆά τε Δηΐπυρόν τε
Μηριόνην τε καὶ Ἀντίλοχον μήστωρας ἀϋτῆς·
sentences.tr:
aue d’ hetairous
Askalaphon t’ esorōn Apharēa te Dēïpyron te
Mērionēn te kai Antilochon mēstōras aÿtēs·
sentences.i: and he called out to his companions, looking at Ascalaphus and Aphareus and Deipyrus and Meriones and Antilochus, masters of the battle-cry;
sentences.n: Idomeneus calls on his men. αὖε is the imperfect of αὔω ‘call out’ (the half-line αὖε δ’ ἑταίρους stands also at 11.461 and is translated the same); ἑταίρους ‘companions’ is the object, and the five names that follow stand in apposition to it, with ἐσορῶν ‘looking at’ (ἐσοράω) saying whom he singles out. Ἀφαρῆα is the accusative of Ἀφαρεύς; Δηΐπυρον and Ἀσκάλαφον are accusatives too. The last line is the one in which Poseidon names the same two among the captains he rouses, at 13.93: μήστωρες ἀϋτῆς is ‘masters of the battle-cry’, μήστωρ being a ‘counsellor, deviser’ and ἀϋτή the war-shout, so ‘those who can plan or rule the cry’ — good in battle. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t: τοὺς ὅ γ’ ἐποτρύνων ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: tous ho g’ epotrynōn epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: Them he, urging on, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Urging them on, he spoke winged words to them:
sentences.n: Idomeneus is the speaker. τοὺς ὅ γ’ ἐποτρύνων: τούς ‘them’ are the five just named, ὅ γε is the pronoun ‘he’, and ἐποτρύνων is the present participle of ἐποτρύνω ‘urge on’. The line is the same as 13.94, where Poseidon addressed the captains he had listed, and is translated the same; ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα as at 462.

sentences.t: δεῦτε φίλοι, καί μ’ οἴῳ ἀμύνετε·
sentences.tr: deute philoi, kai m’ oiōi amynete·
sentences.l: “Hither, friends, and me, alone, defend;
sentences.i: “Come here, friends, and defend me, alone as I am;
sentences.n: Idomeneus’ call for help. δεῦτε is the plural of δεῦρο ‘hither, come’. φίλοι ‘friends’ is the vocative. μ’ is μοι elided, the dative agreeing with οἴῳ (= μόνῳ) ‘alone’, so ἀμύνετε, imperative of ἀμύνω, is ‘defend’ with a person in the dative, as at 464. The speech begins mid-line, and the unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
δείδια δ’ αἰνῶς
Αἰνείαν ἐπιόντα πόδας ταχύν, ὅς μοι ἔπεισιν,
ὃς μάλα καρτερός ἐστι μάχῃ ἔνι φῶτας ἐναίρειν·
sentences.tr:
deidia d’ ainōs
Aineian epionta podas tachyn, hos moi epeisin,
hos mala karteros esti machēi eni phōtas enairein·
sentences.i: I am dreadfully afraid of Aeneas, swift of foot, who is coming on against me, a man very strong at slaying men in battle;
sentences.n: Why he asks: the man who is coming. δείδια is the epic present of δείδω ‘fear’ (a perfect in form, present in sense), with the accusative of what is feared, Αἰνείαν; αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’. ἐπιόντα ‘coming on’; ἔπεισιν is the present of ἔπειμι, ‘comes upon’, with the dative μοι ‘against me’. πόδας ταχύν is ‘swift in feet’, an accusative of respect, the same pattern as πόδας ὠκύς of Achilles but with the word ταχύς ‘swift’. ὃς μάλα καρτερός ἐστι: the second ὅς is a relative that carries on, ‘and he is very strong’; φῶτας ἐναίρειν ‘to slay men’ (ἐναίρω ‘slay’), an infinitive of respect after καρτερός.

sentences.t: καὶ δ’ ἔχει ἥβης ἄνθος, ὅ τε κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον.
sentences.tr: kai d’ echei hēbēs anthos, ho te kratos esti megiston.
sentences.l: and also he has the bloom of youth, which is the greatest strength.
sentences.i: And he has the bloom of youth, which is the greatest strength.
sentences.n: ἥβης ἄνθος ‘the bloom of youth’ is what Idomeneus lacks; he is an older man. καί δ’ ‘and also’; ὅ τε is the relative ‘which’ with epic τε, marking something true in general. κράτος ‘strength’ also means the upper hand or victory, a sense that comes closer in the next line.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ ὁμηλικίη γε γενοίμεθα τῷδ’ ἐπὶ θυμῷ
αἶψά κεν ἠὲ φέροιτο μέγα κράτος, ἠὲ φεροίμην.
sentences.tr:
ei gar homēlikiē ge genoimetha tōid’ epi thymōi
aipsa ken ēe pheroito mega kratos, ēe pheroimēn.
sentences.l:
For if in age equal we were, with this spirit,
quickly either he would carry off great strength, or I would.”
sentences.i: If only we were of an age, with this spirit of mine, either he or I would soon carry off great strength.”
sentences.n: εἰ γάρ with the optative is a wish, ‘if only…’; γενοίμεθα is the aorist optative of γίγνομαι. ὁμηλικίη (printed without an iota, so it could also be read as a nominative predicate) is taken as a dative of respect, ‘in age’, i.e. ‘equal in age’ (elsewhere the same noun means ‘company of one’s own age’). τῷδ’ ἐπὶ θυμῷ ‘on this spirit’ means ‘with this spirit that I have’; ὅδε is the pronoun of the first person, so ‘this’ spirit is the speaker’s own. κεν with the optatives φέροιτο and φεροίμην (middle of φέρω ‘carry off for oneself’) gives the result, ‘he would carry off … or I’. κράτος μέγα ‘great strength’ here is mastery won in the fight. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἕνα φρεσὶ θυμὸν ἔχοντες
πλησίοι ἔστησαν, σάκε’ ὤμοισι κλίναντες.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes hena phresi thymon echontes
plēsioi estēsan, sake’ ōmoisi klinantes.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they all, one spirit in their wits holding,
close together stood, the shields on their shoulders leaning.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all, with a single spirit in their minds, stood close together, resting their shields against their shoulders.
sentences.n: The five come to Idomeneus. ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’: ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο with the final vowel dropped, the τ turned into θ before the rough breathing of the next word. ἕνα … θυμὸν ἔχοντες ‘having one spirit’ means ‘of one mind’; φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν ‘wits, mind’. πλησίοι ‘near’ is an adjective doing the work of an adverb; ἔστησαν is the aorist of ἵστημι in its intransitive sense ‘took their stand’. σάκε’ is σάκεα ‘shields’; ὤμοισι ‘on their shoulders’; κλίναντες ‘leaning’, the shield tilted against the shoulder. The same phrase is at 11.593. The edition begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
Αἰνείας δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐκέκλετο οἷς ἑτάροισι
Δηΐφοβόν τε Πάριν τ’ ἐσορῶν καὶ Ἀγήνορα δῖον,
οἵ οἱ ἅμ’ ἡγεμόνες Τρώων ἔσαν·
sentences.tr:
Aineias d’ heterōthen ekekleto hois hetaroisi
Dēïphobon te Parin t’ esorōn kai Agēnora dion,
hoi hoi ham’ hēgemones Trōōn esan·
sentences.i: And on the other side Aeneas gave orders to his own companions, looking at Deiphobus and Paris and heavenly Agenor, who were leaders of the Trojans along with him;
sentences.n: The Trojan side answers. ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’; ἐκέκλετο ‘called out’ (‘gave orders to’), a reduplicated aorist of κέλομαι; οἷς is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative, and the three names that follow stand in apposition to ἑτάροισι ‘companions’. ἐσορῶν ‘looking at’. In οἵ οἱ ἅμ’ the first οἵ is the relative ‘who’ and the second οἱ (no accent) ‘with him’, with ἅμα ‘along with’; ἔσαν is the epic form of ἦσαν. Δηΐφοβον and Πάριν are the Trojans’ own princes, so ‘leaders’ is the poet’s claim for the three. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
λαοὶ ἕπονθ’, ὡς εἴ τε μετὰ κτίλον ἕσπετο μῆλα
πιόμεν’ ἐκ βοτάνης·
sentences.tr:
autar epeita
laoi heponth’, hōs ei te meta ktilon hespeto mēla
piomen’ ek botanēs·
sentences.i: and after them the troops followed, as flocks follow after the tame ram when they go from the pasture to drink;
sentences.n: The simile of the flock. ἔπειτα ‘then, after them’; ἕπονθ’ is ἕποντο, the final vowel dropped and τ turned into θ before the rough breathing of ὡς; λαοί ‘people’ here are the Trojan troops. ὡς εἴ τε ‘as when’ opens the picture, and ἕσπετο is an aorist used for what happens in general, so English puts it in the present. μῆλα ‘flocks’ is the word for sheep and goats together. κτίλον ‘tame ram’: the word is rare and its sense is not known, ‘tame’ being the traditional gloss. πιόμεν’ is πιόμενα, the future participle of πίνω, ‘to drink’, expressing purpose; ἐκ βοτάνης ‘from the pasture’.

sentences.t: γάνυται δ’ ἄρα τε φρένα ποιμήν·
sentences.tr: ganytai d’ ara te phrena poimēn·
sentences.l: and delighted in his wits is the shepherd;
sentences.i: and the shepherd is delighted in his mind;
sentences.n: γάνυται ‘is delighted’, from γάνυμαι (the sense is of brightening up with joy). φρένα, the accusative of respect, says where, ‘in his wits’, as φρεσί did at 487. ἄρα τε marks a general truth. A line of the same build stands at 8.559, with γέγηθε ‘is glad’ in place of γάνυται. The unit is the last half of line 493.

sentences.t:
ὣς Αἰνείᾳ θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι γεγήθει
ὡς ἴδε λαῶν ἔθνος ἐπισπόμενον ἑοῖ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
hōs Aineiāi thymos eni stēthessi gegēthei
hōs ide laōn ethnos epispomenon heoi autōi.
sentences.l:
so to Aeneas the heart in his breast was glad,
when he saw the company of the people following himself.
sentences.i: So the heart in Aeneas’ breast was glad when he saw the company of the troops following him.
sentences.n: The simile is applied: ὣς … ὡς, the first ‘so’, the second ‘when’. Αἰνείᾳ is the dative of the person whose heart it is; στήθεσσι is the epic dative plural of στῆθος, ‘in the breast’; γεγήθει is the pluperfect of γέγηθα, used here as an imperfect, ‘was glad’. ἔθνος λαῶν ‘company of the people’; ἐπισπόμενον is the aorist participle of ἐφέπομαι ‘follow’; ἑοῖ αὐτῷ is the epic dative of the reflexive with αὐτῷ, ‘following himself’ in person.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀμφ’ Ἀλκαθόῳ αὐτοσχεδὸν ὁρμήθησαν
μακροῖσι ξυστοῖσι·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ amph’ Alkathoōi autoschedon hormēthēsan
makroisi xystoisi·
sentences.l:
And they around Alcathous at close quarters rushed
with long polished spears;
sentences.i: And they rushed at close quarters around Alcathous with their long polished spears;
sentences.n: The two bands close over the body of Alcathous. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are both sides; ἀμφί with the dative ‘around’; ὁρμήθησαν is the aorist passive of ὁρμάω with an active sense, ‘rushed’. αὐτοσχεδόν ‘at close quarters, hand to hand’. ξυστοῖσι is from ξυστόν, a spear, so called from being ‘scraped smooth’, a dative of means, with the epic dative μακροῖσι ‘long’. The edition begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
περὶ στήθεσσι δὲ χαλκὸς
σμερδαλέον κονάβιζε τιτυσκομένων καθ’ ὅμιλον
ἀλλήλων·
sentences.tr:
peri stēthessi de chalkos
smerdaleon konabize tityskomenōn kath’ homilon
allēlōn·
sentences.i: and the bronze about their breasts rang terribly as they took aim at one another through the throng;
sentences.n: περὶ στήθεσσι ‘about the breasts’ (epic dative -εσσι) is the bronze of breastplates and shields. κονάβιζε is the imperfect of κοναβίζω ‘ring, resound’, and σμερδαλέον ‘terribly’ is an adverbial accusative. τιτυσκομένων ἀλλήλων is a genitive absolute, ‘as they took aim at one another’ (τιτύσκομαι ‘aim at’); καθ’ ὅμιλον ‘through the throng’ (κατά ‘down through’). The genitive absolute is split by the line end: ἀλλήλων is the first word of 499. The unit begins in mid-line and ends at the ano teleia after ἀλλήλων.

sentences.t:
δύο δ’ ἄνδρες ἀρήϊοι ἔξοχον ἄλλων
Αἰνείας τε καὶ Ἰδομενεὺς ἀτάλαντοι Ἄρηϊ
ἵεντ’ ἀλλήλων ταμέειν χρόα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr:
dyo d’ andres arēïoi exochon allōn
Aineias te kai Idomeneus atalantoi Arēï
hient’ allēlōn tameein chroa nēleï chalkōi.
sentences.l:
and two men, warlike, outstanding beyond the others,
Aeneas and Idomeneus, the equals of Ares,
were eager of one another to cut the skin with pitiless bronze.
sentences.i: and two warlike men, outstanding above the rest, Aeneas and Idomeneus, the equals of Ares, were eager to cut one another’s skin with pitiless bronze.
sentences.n: Out of the throng the leaders come to grips. δύο … ἄνδρες ‘two men’ are named in apposition, Αἰνείας τε καὶ Ἰδομενεύς. ἀρήϊοι ‘warlike’; ἔξοχον ἄλλων ‘outstanding beyond the others’, with the genitive of comparison. ἀτάλαντοι Ἄρηϊ ‘equals of Ares’ (dative Ἄρηϊ), the stock phrase for a match for the war-god. ἵεντ’ is ἵεντο, imperfect middle of ἵημι, ‘were eager’, with the infinitive ταμέειν (epic = τεμεῖν) ‘to cut’; ἀλλήλων ‘of one another’ goes with χρόα ‘skin’. νηλέϊ is the epic dative of νηλεής ‘pitiless’.

sentences.t: Αἰνείας δὲ πρῶτος ἀκόντισεν Ἰδομενῆος·
sentences.tr: Aineias de prōtos akontisen Idomenēos·
sentences.l: And Aeneas first cast at Idomeneus;
sentences.i: Aeneas was the first to cast at Idomeneus;
sentences.n: ἀκόντισεν is the aorist of ἀκοντίζω ‘cast a javelin’, taking the genitive Ἰδομενῆος (epic genitive -ῆος) of the man aimed at. The Greek gives no object; the spear is named in the next line. πρῶτος ‘first’ means Aeneas throws before Idomeneus does.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἄντα ἰδὼν ἠλεύατο χάλκεον ἔγχος,
αἰχμὴ δ’ Αἰνείαο κραδαινομένη κατὰ γαίης
ᾤχετ’, ἐπεί ῥ’ ἅλιον στιβαρῆς ἀπὸ χειρὸς ὄρουσεν.
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men anta idōn ēleuato chalkeon enchos,
aichmē d’ Aineiao kradainomenē kata gaiēs
ōichet’, epei rh’ halion stibarēs apo cheiros orousen.
sentences.l:
But he, looking straight at it, avoided the bronze spear,
and the point of Aeneas, quivering, into the earth
went off, since in vain from his stout hand it had darted.
sentences.i: But Idomeneus, seeing it coming straight at him, avoided the bronze spear, and the point of Aeneas’ spear went off, quivering, into the ground, since it had sped in vain from his stout hand.
sentences.n: Idomeneus dodges. ὃ μέν is the pronoun ‘he’, Idomeneus, who is not named in this unit; ἄντα ἰδών ‘seeing it straight in front of him’; ἠλεύατο ‘avoided’ is the aorist of ἀλέομαι. The line is the one Idomeneus used in the previous part, at 13.404, and is translated the same. αἰχμὴ δ’ Αἰνείαο ‘the point of Aeneas’ (spear)’ stands for the whole weapon; κραδαινομένη is the present participle of κραδαίνω ‘quiver’; ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘was gone’; κατὰ γαίης ‘down into the earth’ with the genitive. ἅλιον is ‘in vain’ (an adverb; not the ἅλιος ‘of the sea’); στιβαρῆς ‘stout’ is the stock epithet of the hand; ὄρουσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι, ‘darted’.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ ἄρα Οἰνόμαον βάλε γαστέρα μέσσην,
ῥῆξε δὲ θώρηκος γύαλον, διὰ δ’ ἔντερα χαλκὸς
ἤφυσ’·
sentences.tr:
Idomeneus d’ ara Oinomaon bale gastera messēn,
rhēxe de thōrēkos gyalon, dia d’ entera chalkos
ēphys’·
sentences.i: And Idomeneus hit Oenomaus in the middle of the belly and broke the hollow of his breastplate, and the bronze drew his bowels out through it;
sentences.n: Idomeneus strikes back. Οἰνόμαον is the object of βάλε ‘hit’, with a second accusative γαστέρα μέσσην ‘the middle belly’ for the part struck. ῥῆξε is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’; θώρηκος γύαλον ‘the hollow of the breastplate’, the rounded front of the armour. διὰ δ’ … ἤφυσ’ is διήφυσε with the preverb separated (tmesis), ‘drew out through’: ἀφύσσω is a verb for drawing liquid, so the bowels pour out. The unit ends at the ano teleia after ἤφυσ’.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐν κονίῃσι πεσὼν ἕλε γαῖαν ἀγοστῷ.
sentences.tr: ho d’ en koniēisi pesōn hele gaian agostōi.
sentences.l: and he, in the dust having fallen, took the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.i: and he fell in the dust and clutched the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.n: Oenomaus falls. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’; πεσών is the aorist participle of πίπτω ‘fall’; ἕλε γαῖαν ἀγοστῷ is literally ‘took the earth with the ἀγοστός’, a rare word whose sense is not known: ‘the crook of the arm’ is the traditional guess, ‘the hollow of the hand’ another. The same line comes again at 520. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ ἐκ μὲν νέκυος δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος
ἐσπάσατ’, οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ ἄλλα δυνήσατο τεύχεα καλὰ
ὤμοιιν ἀφελέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
Idomeneus d’ ek men nekyos dolichoskion enchos
espasat’, oud’ ar’ et’ alla dynēsato teuchea kala
ōmoiin aphelesthai·
sentences.i: Idomeneus pulled his long-shadowed spear out of the corpse, but he could not take off the rest of the fine armour as well from the shoulders;
sentences.n: He gets his spear back but cannot strip the body. ἐκ … νέκυος ‘from the corpse’; ἐσπάσατ’ is ἐσπάσατο, aorist middle of σπάω ‘pull’, the middle because the spear is his own. δολιχόσκιον ‘long-shadowed’ is the stock epithet of the spear. οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ ἄλλα … τεύχεα ‘nor, besides, the other armour’: ἔτι can also mean ‘any longer’, and the reason given next fits either. ὤμοιιν is the dual genitive of ὦμος ‘shoulder’, ‘from the two shoulders’; ἀφελέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀφαιρέω ‘take off’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἐπείγετο γὰρ βελέεσσιν.
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἔμπεδα γυῖα ποδῶν ἦν ὁρμηθέντι,
οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ἐπαΐξαι μεθ’ ἑὸν· βέλος οὔτ’ ἀλέασθαι.
sentences.tr:
epeigeto gar beleessin.
ou gar et’ empeda guia podōn ēn hormēthenti,
out’ ar’ epaïxai meth’ heon· belos out’ aleasthai.
sentences.l:
for he was pressed hard with shafts.
For no longer firm were the limbs of his feet, when he set off,
neither to dash after his own, nor to avoid a shaft.
sentences.i: He was hard pressed by their shafts, for his legs were no longer firm when he made a rush, and he could neither dash after his own nor avoid a shaft.
sentences.n: Why he cannot strip the dead man: he is under fire and his legs have lost their spring. ἐπείγετο is the imperfect passive of ἐπείγω ‘press hard’; βελέεσσιν is the epic dative plural of βέλος ‘shaft’. ἔμπεδα γυῖα ποδῶν ‘firm limbs of the feet’ means the legs, with ὁρμηθέντι ‘to him having set off’ (aorist passive participle of ὁρμάω), ‘when he made a rush’. οὔτ’ … οὔτ’ ‘neither … nor’ with the infinitives ἐπαΐξαι (aorist of ἐπαΐσσω ‘dash at, after’) and ἀλέασθαι ‘to avoid’. The edition prints a stop after ἑόν, which leaves ἑὸν ‘his own’ standing alone (his own cast, understood) and βέλος as the object of ἀλέασθαι; the grammar is not quite certain. The unit begins in mid-line and has the stop inside it.

sentences.t:
τώ ῥα καὶ ἐν σταδίῃ μὲν ἀμύνετο νηλεὲς ἦμαρ,
τρέσσαι δ’ οὐκ ἔτι ῥίμφα πόδες φέρον ἐκ πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
tō rha kai en stadiēi men amyneto nēlees ēmar,
tressai d’ ouk eti rhimpha podes pheron ek polemoio.
sentences.l:
Therefore indeed in the standing fight he warded off the pitiless day,
but to flee no longer nimbly did his feet bear him from the war.
sentences.i: And so in the fight where men stand their ground he could ward off the pitiless day, but his feet no longer carried him nimbly out of the war to flee.
sentences.n: τώ ῥα ‘and so, then’ draws the conclusion. σταδίῃ is the adjective ‘standing’ (the noun ὑσμίνῃ ‘battle’ understood), a fight in which men stand their ground, as at 13.314. ἀμύνετο is the imperfect middle of ἀμύνω, ‘ward off from oneself’, with the accusative νηλεὲς ἦμαρ ‘the pitiless day’, the day of death. μέν … δέ sets what he can do against what he cannot. τρέσσαι is τρέσαι, ‘to flee in fear’, with the double σ for the metre; ῥίμφα ‘nimbly’; φέρον is the unaugmented imperfect of φέρω.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δὲ βάδην ἀπιόντος ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ
Δηΐφοβος·
sentences.tr:
tou de badēn apiontos akontise douri phaeinōi
Dēïphobos·
sentences.l:
And at him, going away at a walk, cast with a shining spear
Deiphobus;
sentences.i: As Idomeneus went off at a walk, Deiphobus cast at him with his shining spear;
sentences.n: τοῦ … ἀπιόντος ‘as he went away’ is the genitive that names the man aimed at, as with ἀκόντισε in 502. βάδην ‘at a walk, step by step’ is the slow retreat his legs allow. δουρὶ φαεινῷ ‘shining spear’ is the stock phrase, translated the same each time. The name Δηΐφοβος is held to the start of the next line, and the unit ends at the ano teleia after it.

sentences.t: δὴ γάρ οἱ ἔχεν κότον ἐμμενὲς αἰεί.
sentences.tr: dē gar hoi echen koton emmenes aiei.
sentences.l: for indeed against him he held resentment, steadily, always.
sentences.i: for he held a resentment against him unceasingly.
sentences.n: δὴ γάρ ‘for indeed’. ἔχεν is ἔχε (movable -ν), the imperfect of ἔχω; κότον ἔχειν τινί ‘to hold a resentment against someone’, with the dative οἱ ‘against him’. κότος is a lasting resentment, kept apart from χόλος ‘anger’. ἐμμενές ‘steadily’ and αἰεί ‘always’ are two adverbs, the pair that stands also at 10.361, the second making the first stronger. The lines give no reason for the grudge. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε καὶ τόθ’ ἅμαρτεν, ὃ δ’ Ἀσκάλαφον βάλε δουρὶ
υἱὸν Ἐνυαλίοιο·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho ge kai toth’ hamarten, ho d’ Askalaphon bale douri
huion Enyalioio·
sentences.l:
But he missed even then, and Ascalaphus he hit with the spear,
the son of Enyalius;
sentences.i: But even then he missed, and he hit Ascalaphus, son of Enyalius, with his spear;
sentences.n: Deiphobus’ cast fails against Idomeneus but kills another man. ἀλλ’ ὅ γε καὶ τόθ’ ἅμαρτεν ‘but he missed even then’ (ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’); ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is the same man, Deiphobus. Ἀσκάλαφον is one of the five companions Idomeneus called at 478. Ἐνυαλίοιο is the epic genitive of Ἐνυάλιος, a war-god’s name, who is Ares here, as the next lines show: the man’s father is Ares at 521–522. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
δι’ ὤμου δ’ ὄβριμον ἔγχος
ἔσχεν·
sentences.tr:
di’ ōmou d’ obrimon enchos
eschen·
sentences.l:
and through the shoulder the mighty spear
held;
sentences.i: and the mighty spear held fast through his shoulder;
sentences.n: δι’ ὤμου ‘through the shoulder’ (διά elided before ὤμου). ὄβριμον ἔγχος ‘mighty spear’ is the stock phrase, translated each time. ἔσχεν is the aorist of ἔχω ‘hold’, used intransitively: the spear stayed fixed. The unit begins in mid-line and ends at the ano teleia after ἔσχεν.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐν κονίῃσι πεσὼν ἕλε γαῖαν ἀγοστῷ.
sentences.tr: ho d’ en koniēisi pesōn hele gaian agostōi.
sentences.l: and he, in the dust having fallen, took the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.i: and he fell in the dust and clutched the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.n: Ascalaphus dies as Oenomaus did: the line is the same as 508 and is translated the same (ἀγοστῷ is of unknown sense, ‘the crook of the arm’ the traditional guess).

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα πώ τι πέπυστο βριήπυος ὄβριμος Ἄρης
υἷος ἑοῖο πεσόντος ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ,
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara pō ti pepysto briēpyos obrimos Arēs
huios heoio pesontos eni kraterēi hysminēi,
sentences.l:
But not yet at all had learned loud-voiced, mighty Ares
of his own son fallen in strong battle,
sentences.i: Ares, loud-voiced and mighty, had not yet learned that his own son had fallen in strong battle,
sentences.n: Where the war-god is. οὐδ’ ἄρα πώ τι ‘and not yet at all’; πέπυστο is the pluperfect of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn’, ‘had learned’, with the genitive υἷος ἑοῖο πεσόντος ‘of his son fallen’, a participle in the genitive where English has a ‘that’ clause. ἑοῖο is the epic genitive of the possessive ἑός ‘his own’. βριήπυος is found only here, and its formation is not certain: the second part is probably ἠπύω ‘call out’ and the first βρι- ‘strong’, so ‘loud-voiced’ rests on that guess. ὄβριμος ‘mighty’; κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ ‘strong battle’, epic dative.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἄρ’ ἄκρῳ Ὀλύμπῳ ὑπὸ χρυσέοισι νέφεσσιν
ἧστο Διὸς βουλῇσιν ἐελμένος, ἔνθά περ ἄλλοι
ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἦσαν ἐεργόμενοι πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
all’ ho g’ ar’ akrōi Olympōi hypo chryseoisi nephessin
hēsto Dios boulēisin eelmenos, entha per alloi
athanatoi theoi ēsan eergomenoi polemoio.
sentences.l:
but he, on the peak of Olympus, beneath golden clouds,
sat, by the plans of Zeus hemmed in, where also the other
immortal gods were, kept from the war.
sentences.i: but he sat on the peak of Olympus, beneath golden clouds, hemmed in by the plans of Zeus, where the other immortal gods also were, kept from the war.
sentences.n: Ares is not at the fighting but on Olympus. ἄκρῳ Ὀλύμπῳ ‘on the topmost Olympus’ (dative of place, no preposition); ὑπὸ … νέφεσσιν ‘beneath clouds’, χρυσέοισι νέφεσσιν ‘golden clouds’ (epic datives). ἧστο is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’. ἐελμένος, perfect passive participle of εἴλω ‘hem in’, goes with Διὸς βουλῇσιν ‘by the plans of Zeus’ (plural, epic -ῃσιν): the plans of Zeus keep him in. ἔνθά περ ‘just where’; ἐεργόμενοι is the passive participle of ἐέργω ‘keep from, shut out’, so the other gods are kept back from the war, too. What the plans are is not said here.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἀμφ’ Ἀσκαλάφῳ αὐτοσχεδὸν ὁρμήθησαν·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ amph’ Askalaphōi autoschedon hormēthēsan·
sentences.l: And they around Ascalaphus at close quarters rushed;
sentences.i: And they rushed at close quarters around Ascalaphus;
sentences.n: A new struggle begins over a new body. The line is the one at 496, with Ascalaphus for Alcathous, and is translated the same; see there for the forms. The edition begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
Δηΐφοβος μὲν ἀπ’ Ἀσκαλάφου πήληκα φαεινὴν
ἥρπασε, Μηριόνης δὲ θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ
δουρὶ βραχίονα τύψεν ἐπάλμενος, ἐκ δ’ ἄρα χειρὸς
αὐλῶπις τρυφάλεια χαμαὶ βόμβησε πεσοῦσα.
sentences.tr:
Dēïphobos men ap’ Askalaphou pēlēka phaeinēn
hērpase, Mērionēs de thoōi atalantos Arēï
douri brachiona typsen epalmenos, ek d’ ara cheiros
aulōpis tryphaleia chamai bombēse pesousa.
sentences.l:
Deiphobus from Ascalaphus the shining helmet
snatched, and Meriones, the equal of swift Ares,
with his spear struck his arm, springing upon him, and from his hand
the tubed helm to the ground boomed, falling.
sentences.i: Deiphobus snatched the shining helmet from Ascalaphus, and Meriones, the equal of swift Ares, sprang upon him and struck his arm with his spear, and the tubed helmet fell from his hand and boomed on the ground.
sentences.n: Deiphobus is the first to strip the dead man, and is punished. Δηΐφοβος μέν … Μηριόνης δέ sets the two against each other. πήληκα, accusative of πήληξ, is a ‘helmet’, like κόρυς at 544 and τρυφάλεια here; ἀπ’ Ἀσκαλάφου ‘from Ascalaphus’; ἥρπασε ‘snatched’. θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ ‘equal to swift Ares’ is the same phrase as at 13.295. τύψεν is τύψε with movable -ν; βραχίονα ‘arm’ is the part struck; ἐπάλμενος is the aorist participle of ἐφάλλομαι ‘spring upon’. ἐκ … χειρός ‘from his hand’ is Deiphobus’ hand, with the helmet he had taken. αὐλῶπις τρυφάλεια ‘tubed helm’: αὐλῶπις is probably from αὐλός ‘tube, pipe’, but what the tube is is not known, and τρυφάλεια has no known origin. βόμβησε ‘boomed’ is a deep hollow sound; πεσοῦσα ‘falling’.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δ’ ἐξ αὖτις ἐπάλμενος αἰγυπιὸς ὣς
ἐξέρυσε πρυμνοῖο βραχίονος ὄβριμον ἔγχος,
ἂψ δ’ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο.
sentences.tr:
Mērionēs d’ ex autis epalmenos aigypios hōs
exeryse prymnoio brachionos obrimon enchos,
aps d’ hetarōn eis ethnos echazeto.
sentences.l:
And Meriones, springing again like a vulture,
drew out from the base of the arm the mighty spear,
and back into the company of his companions he drew away.
sentences.i: And Meriones sprang in again, like a vulture, and drew his mighty spear out from the base of the arm, and drew back into the company of his companions.
sentences.n: Meriones recovers his weapon and retires. ἐξ αὖτις ‘once more’; ἐπάλμενος as at 529. αἰγυπιὸς ὣς ‘like a vulture’: ὣς is placed after its noun. ἐξέρυσε is the aorist of ἐξερύω ‘draw out’; πρυμνοῖο βραχίονος ‘from the base of the arm’, the genitive of the place from which (πρυμνός is the hindmost or lowest part, the root of a limb). ἂψ δ’ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο, ‘back into the company of his companions he drew away’, is the first half of the line said of Alexander at 3.32 and of Eurypylus at 11.585 (there followed by κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων ‘avoiding death’), and of Meriones at 13.164; it is translated as at 11.585 and 13.164. The unit ends at the full stop in mid-line 533.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ Πολίτης
αὐτοκασίγνητος περὶ μέσσῳ χεῖρε τιτήνας
ἐξῆγεν πολέμοιο δυσηχέος,
sentences.tr:
ton de Politēs
autokasignētos peri messōi cheire titēnas
exēgen polemoio dysēcheos,
sentences.l:
and him Polites,
his own brother, around his middle his two arms stretching,
led out of the ill-sounding war,
sentences.i: and his own brother Polites, with his two arms stretched round his waist, led him out of the ill-sounding war,
sentences.n: Deiphobus is taken from the fight. τόν ‘him’ is Deiphobus, the man struck at 529; αὐτοκασίγνητος ‘own brother’ says whose brother Polites is, though the unit does not name him again. περὶ μέσσῳ ‘around the middle’; χεῖρε is a dual, ‘the two arms’, and τιτήνας is the aorist participle of τιταίνω ‘stretch’. ἐξῆγεν ‘was leading out’, imperfect of ἐξάγω. δυσηχέος ‘ill-sounding’ (δυσ- ‘ill’ and ἦχος ‘sound’): the war is thought of as noise. The sentence runs five lines, so the unit is cut at the comma after δυσηχέος, and it begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ἵκεθ’ ἵππους
ὠκέας, οἵ οἱ ὄπισθε μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο
ἕστασαν ἡνίοχόν τε καὶ ἅρματα ποικίλ’ ἔχοντες·
sentences.tr:
ophr’ hiketh’ hippous
ōkeas, hoi hoi opisthe machēs ēde ptolemoio
hestasan hēniochon te kai harmata poikil’ echontes·
sentences.i: until he came to the swift horses that stood for him behind the fight and the war, with their charioteer and their intricate chariot;
sentences.n: ὄφρ’ ἵκεθ’ ‘until he reached’ (ἵκεθ’ is ἵκετο, the final vowel dropped and τ turned into θ), with the accusative ἵππους ‘horses’. οἵ is the relative ‘which’, and οἱ (no accent) ‘for him’, the wounded man. ὄπισθε μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο ‘behind the fight and the war’. ἕστασαν ‘stood’ is the pluperfect of ἵστημι in the sense of a past state; ἔχοντες ‘having’ means they stood with charioteer and chariot, as a team at the ready. ποικίλ’ is ποικίλα ‘intricate’; ἅρματα, plural in form, is one chariot. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οἳ τόν γε προτὶ ἄστυ φέρον βαρέα στενάχοντα
τειρόμενον·
sentences.tr:
hoi ton ge proti asty pheron barea stenachonta
teiromenon·
sentences.l:
and they to the city bore him, heavily groaning,
worn down;
sentences.i: and they carried him to the city, groaning heavily, worn down;
sentences.n: οἳ ‘they’ are the horses. φέρον is the unaugmented imperfect of φέρω ‘bear’; τόν γε ‘him’; προτὶ ἄστυ ‘to the city’ (προτί is the epic form of πρός). βαρέα στενάχοντα ‘groaning heavily’ and τειρόμενον ‘worn down’ agree with τόν, so the man groaning is Deiphobus. βαρέα στενάχοντα is the phrase used of Hypsenor at 13.423, and is translated the same.

sentences.t: κατὰ δ’ αἷμα νεουτάτου ἔρρεε χειρός.
sentences.tr: kata d’ haima neoutatou erree cheiros.
sentences.l: and down the blood from the freshly wounded hand flowed.
sentences.i: and the blood flowed down from the freshly wounded arm.
sentences.n: κατά is separated from ἔρρεε, the imperfect of ῥέω ‘flow’ (tmesis), ‘flowed down’. νεουτάτου ‘freshly wounded’ (νέος ‘new’ and οὐτάω ‘wound’) agrees with χειρός; χείρ is the hand and also the whole arm, as here, where the wound is in the upper arm (529). The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι μάρναντο, βοὴ δ’ ἄσβεστος ὀρώρει.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ alloi marnanto, boē d’ asbestos orōrei.
sentences.l: And the others fought on, and an unquenchable war-cry had arisen.
sentences.i: The rest fought on, and a war-cry that would never go out had arisen.
sentences.n: Elsewhere the fighting goes on. οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι ‘and the others’; μάρναντο is the unaugmented imperfect of μάρναμαι ‘fight’. ἄσβεστος ‘unquenchable’ is ἀ- ‘not’ and σβέννυμι ‘put out’; ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι with the sense ‘had arisen’, ‘was up’. The edition begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Αἰνέας Ἀφαρῆα Καλητορίδην ἐπορούσας
λαιμὸν τύψ’ ἐπὶ οἷ τετραμμένον ὀξέϊ δουρί·
sentences.tr:
enth’ Aineas Apharēa Kalētoridēn eporousas
laimon typs’ epi hoi tetrammenon oxeï douri·
sentences.l:
Then Aeneas, rushing on Aphareus, Caletor’s-son,
struck him in the throat, turned toward him, with a sharp spear;
sentences.i: Then Aeneas rushed on Aphareus, son of Caletor, who had turned toward him, and struck him in the throat with a sharp spear;
sentences.n: Aeneas’ first kill in this fight. Ἀφαρῆα is the accusative of Ἀφαρεύς, one of the companions Idomeneus called at 478; Καλητορίδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Caletor’. Αἰνέας is the shorter spelling of Αἰνείας, as printed here. ἐπορούσας is the aorist participle of ἐπορούω ‘rush upon’; λαιμόν ‘throat’ is the part struck, as γαστέρα was at 506; τύψ’ is τύψε. ἐπὶ οἷ τετραμμένον ‘turned toward him’: οἷ is the epic dative of the reflexive pronoun and τετραμμένον the perfect passive participle of τρέπω, so Aphareus had turned to face Aeneas. ὀξέϊ is the epic dative of ὀξύς ‘sharp’.

sentences.t:
ἐκλίνθη δ’ ἑτέρωσε κάρη, ἐπὶ δ’ ἀσπὶς ἑάφθη
καὶ κόρυς, ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ θάνατος χύτο θυμοραϊστής.
sentences.tr:
eklinthē d’ heterōse karē, epi d’ aspis heaphthē
kai korys, amphi de hoi thanatos chyto thymoraïstēs.
sentences.l:
and his head leaned to the other side, and upon him shield
and helmet fell, and about him death was poured, life-destroying.
sentences.i: His head slumped to one side, and his shield and helmet fell upon him, and death, the destroyer of life, was poured about him.
sentences.n: Aphareus dies. ἐκλίνθη ‘leaned’ is the aorist passive of κλίνω; ἑτέρωσε ‘to the other side’ (the -σε ending gives direction); κάρη is a neuter noun, ‘head’. ἐπὶ δ’ … ἑάφθη is ἐπεάφθη with the preverb separated (tmesis), a rare aorist passive of ἅπτω; its sense is not certain, ‘was laid upon’ or ‘fell upon’ being the guesses, and the shield and the helmet (κόρυς) are its two subjects. ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ … χύτο ‘about him was poured’ (χύτο is the aorist middle of χέω): death is a thing that can be poured about a man, as a haze is poured over the eyes of Sarpedon when he faints at 5.696. θυμοραϊστής is θυμός ‘life, spirit’ with ῥαίω ‘shatter, destroy’, ‘life-destroying’.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δὲ Θόωνα μεταστρεφθέντα δοκεύσας
οὔτασ’ ἐπαΐξας, ἀπὸ δὲ φλέβα πᾶσαν ἔκερσεν,
sentences.tr:
Antilochos de Thoōna metastrephthenta dokeusas
outas’ epaïxas, apo de phleba pasan ekersen,
sentences.l:
And Antilochus, watching for Thoon as he turned round,
wounded him, rushing at him, and the vein, the whole of it, cut away,
sentences.i: And Antilochus, having watched Thoon turn round, rushed at him and wounded him, and cut away the whole vein,
sentences.n: Antilochus’ kill. Θόωνα is the accusative of Θόων; nothing more is told of him here. μεταστρεφθέντα is the aorist passive participle of μεταστρέφω ‘turn round’; δοκεύσας ‘having watched’, aorist participle of δοκεύω. οὔτασ’ is οὔτασε ‘wounded’ (οὐτάω); ἐπαΐξας ‘rushing at’ (cf. ἐπαΐξαι at 513). ἀπὸ … ἔκερσεν is tmesis for ἀπέκερσεν, ‘cut away’, from κείρω ‘shear, cut’. φλέβα πᾶσαν ‘the whole vein’, which the next line identifies.

sentences.t: ἥ τ’ ἀνὰ νῶτα θέουσα διαμπερὲς αὐχέν’ ἱκάνει·
sentences.tr: hē t’ ana nōta theousa diamperes auchen’ hikanei·
sentences.l: which up along the back running right through reaches the neck;
sentences.i: the one that runs up along the back right through to the neck;
sentences.n: The vein is described as a general fact, which is why the verbs are in the present. ἥ is the relative ‘which’ with epic τε; ἀνὰ νῶτα ‘up along the back’; θέουσα ‘running’ (θέω); διαμπερές ‘right through’; αὐχέν’ is αὐχένα ‘neck’, elided; ἱκάνει ‘reaches’.

sentences.t: τὴν ἀπὸ πᾶσαν ἔκερσεν·
sentences.tr: tēn apo pasan ekersen·
sentences.l: that, the whole of it, he cut away;
sentences.i: he cut it away, the whole of it;
sentences.n: τὴν ἀπὸ πᾶσαν ἔκερσεν takes up the verb of 546 again after the description of the vein: τήν is the article as a pronoun, ‘it’; ἀπό is the preverb of ἔκερσεν standing apart (tmesis). The repeated words stress that the whole vein was severed. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line, after ἔκερσεν.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὕπτιος ἐν κονίῃσι
κάππεσεν, ἄμφω χεῖρε φίλοις ἑτάροισι πετάσσας.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ hyptios en koniēisi
kappesen, amphō cheire philois hetaroisi petassas.
sentences.l:
and he on his back in the dust
fell down, both hands to his dear companions spreading out.
sentences.i: and he fell down on his back in the dust, spreading out both hands to his dear companions.
sentences.n: Thoon falls. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’; ὕπτιος ‘on his back’; ἐν κονίῃσι ‘in the dust’, the epic dative plural of κονίη. κάππεσεν is κατέπεσεν ‘fell down’, with κατά assimilated to the following π. ἄμφω χεῖρε ‘both hands’ is a dual accusative; φίλοις ἑτάροισι is the dative of whom the hands are stretched to; πετάσσας ‘spreading out’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δ’ ἐπόρουσε, καὶ αἴνυτο τεύχε’ ἀπ’ ὤμων
παπταίνων·
sentences.tr:
Antilochos d’ eporouse, kai ainyto teuche’ ap’ ōmōn
paptainōn·
sentences.l:
And Antilochus sprang upon him, and was taking the armour from his shoulders,
glancing about;
sentences.i: And Antilochus sprang upon him and began to strip the armour from his shoulders, glancing about;
sentences.n: Antilochus strips the body, but watchfully. ἐπόρουσε is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘spring upon’; αἴνυτο is the imperfect of αἴνυμαι ‘take’, so ‘was taking, began to strip’; τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’; ἀπ’ ὤμων ‘from the shoulders’. παπταίνων ‘glancing about’, the present participle of παπταίνω. The words from ἐπόρουσε to ὤμων are those said of Eurypylus at 11.580, and are translated the same. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δὲ περισταδὸν ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος
οὔταζον σάκος εὐρὺ παναίολον, οὐδὲ δύναντο
εἴσω ἐπιγράψαι τέρενα χρόα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ
Ἀντιλόχου·
sentences.tr:
Trōes de peristadon allothen allos
outazon sakos eury panaiolon, oude dynanto
eisō epigrapsai terena chroa nēleï chalkōi
Antilochou·
sentences.l:
but the Trojans, standing round, one from here, one from there,
kept thrusting at his broad shield, all-glancing, and could not
inside it graze the tender skin with pitiless bronze
of Antilochus;
sentences.i: while the Trojans, standing all round, one from one side and another from another, kept stabbing at his broad, all-glancing shield, and could not reach inside to graze Antilochus’ tender skin with the pitiless bronze;
sentences.n: The Trojans close in, and fail. περισταδόν ‘standing round’ is an adverb; ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος ‘one from one side, another from another’. οὔταζον is the imperfect of οὐτάζω ‘thrust at, wound’, the repeated attempts. σάκος εὐρύ ‘broad shield’; παναίολον ‘all-glancing’ (αἰόλος is ‘quick-moving, glancing’), whether ‘gleaming’ or ‘many-coloured’ is not certain; the word is also used of a belt at 4.186. εἴσω ‘inside’, i.e. past the shield; ἐπιγράψαι, aorist infinitive of ἐπιγράφω, ‘graze, scratch the surface of’; τέρενα χρόα ‘tender skin’; νηλέϊ ‘pitiless’. The genitive Ἀντιλόχου, which depends on χρόα, is held to the start of the next line. The unit begins in mid-line and ends at the ano teleia after Ἀντιλόχου.

sentences.t:
πέρι γάρ ῥα Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων
Νέστορος υἱὸν ἔρυτο καὶ ἐν πολλοῖσι βέλεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
peri gar rha Poseidaōn enosichthōn
Nestoros huion eryto kai en polloisi belessin.
sentences.l:
for exceedingly Poseidon, the earth-shaker,
the son of Nestor guarded, even amid many shafts.
sentences.i: for Poseidon, the earth-shaker, guarded Nestor’s son beyond all others, even amid many shafts.
sentences.n: Why the Trojans fail. πέρι is the adverb ‘exceedingly, beyond others’ (not the preposition); ἔρυτο is the imperfect of ἐρύομαι ‘guard’. ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’ is Poseidon’s stock epithet, translated each time. Νέστορος υἱόν ‘the son of Nestor’ is Antilochus, who is not named again. καὶ ἐν πολλοῖσι βέλεσσιν ‘even amid many shafts’, with βέλεσσιν the epic dative plural of βέλος. As in the previous part, Poseidon is working on the Achaeans’ side. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ ποτ’ ἄνευ δηΐων ἦν, ἀλλὰ κατ’ αὐτοὺς
στρωφᾶτ’·
sentences.tr:
ou men gar pot’ aneu dēïōn ēn, alla kat’ autous
strōphat’·
sentences.l:
For never was he without enemies, but among them
he kept turning about;
sentences.i: For he was never without enemies; he kept turning about among them;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ ‘for truly not’, the particles strengthening the denial; ποτ’ ‘ever’. ἄνευ δηΐων ‘without enemies’: δήϊος ‘hostile’ is used as a noun, in the genitive after ἄνευ. κατ’ αὐτούς ‘among them’, i.e. among the enemies. στρωφᾶτ’ is στρωφᾶτο, the imperfect middle of στρωφάω ‘turn about’, in its epic form (a frequentative of the verb that is στρέφω in Attic). The unit ends at the ano teleia after the first word of 557.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ οἱ ἔγχος ἔχ’ ἀτρέμας, ἀλλὰ μάλ’ αἰεὶ
σειόμενον ἐλέλικτο·
sentences.tr:
oude hoi enchos ech’ atremas, alla mal’ aiei
seiomenon elelikto·
sentences.l:
nor did his spear stay motionless, but very constantly
being shaken it was whirled;
sentences.i: and his spear never stayed motionless, but was always being shaken and whirled;
sentences.n: οὐδέ οἱ ἔγχος ἔχ’ ἀτρέμας ‘nor did his spear stay motionless’: ἔχ’ is ἔχε, the imperfect of ἔχω used intransitively, ‘stayed’; οἱ ‘his’ (dative of possession); ἀτρέμας ‘motionless’. σειόμενον is the present passive participle of σείω ‘shake’; ἐλέλικτο is the pluperfect passive of ἑλίσσω ‘whirl’, ‘was kept whirling’. The unit begins in mid-line and ends at the ano teleia after ἐλέλικτο.

sentences.t:
τιτύσκετο δὲ φρεσὶν ᾗσιν
ἤ τευ ἀκοντίσσαι, ἠὲ σχεδὸν ὁρμηθῆναι.
sentences.tr:
titysketo de phresin hēisin
ē teu akontissai, ēe schedon hormēthēnai.
sentences.l:
and he was taking aim in his own wits
either to cast at someone, or to rush near.
sentences.i: and in his own mind he was aiming either to cast at someone or to rush in close.
sentences.n: τιτύσκετο is the imperfect middle of τιτύσκομαι ‘aim, take aim’, here followed by two infinitives, ‘was bent on’. φρεσὶν ᾗσιν ‘in his own wits’: ᾗσιν is the possessive ὅς ‘his own’ (epic dative plural -ῃσιν), not the relative. τευ is τινός, ‘at someone’, the genitive of the target, as at 502; ἀκοντίσσαι is ἀκοντίσαι with the double σ for the metre. ἠὲ σχεδὸν ὁρμηθῆναι ‘or to rush close’ (aorist passive infinitive of ὁρμάω with active sense; σχεδόν ‘near, at close quarters’). The unit begins in mid-line.
